blocks.x: We got testing one, two, one, one, two, one, two, testing one, two. Okay, this is an interview with Percy Stovall, and the date of today is December, what's today?
The date of the 27th.

27th of December, 1977, and we're at his house on 3rd Street, 1731. 31, right. 31, 31, 3rd Street. Percy, why don't we, since I know we want to talk about Guitar Slim, but I wanted to maybe get some background on you and what, you know, your role in the business. Why don't you give me your birthday?
My birthday is October 17, 1906. 1906, well you've been around for a long time, but 71 years.
Yeah, I didn't know you've been around, aren't you?
Right.
What section of town were you born in?
Well, I wasn't born in New Orleans. I was born in Jackson, Mississippi. Oh. I've been here for 48 years, though.
Well, how'd you get to New Orleans?

What were you? Well, I just got tired of Mississippi and came to New Orleans and been here ever since. Of course, I've lived in Los Angeles. I've lived in Buffalo, New York since that particular time, but this is what I call home. Here's home, you see.
What did you do in Jackson?

Well, in Jackson, I was with my parents was a farmer. I was there when I was about 18 years old, you see. My parents was a farmer there. Outside of Jackson? Outside of Jackson. A little town called Canton, Mississippi. Yeah.
So you all, you raised?
Raised on that farm there until I was 18, then I came to New Orleans.
Well, how'd you get interested in doing music, a book?
Well, when I came here, I always was interested in music, I always liked it, you know, I never could play it. I took a piano lesson for years. I never could play it. Yeah.
What did you, I mean you tried to play in that musical instrument?
I tried piano for years, never could play it. Never could play piano.
When you were growing up, what music, who'd you listen to when you were growing up?

Well, in that particular time, most things you were listening was church music, you know. I played choir, the lady who played for the choir, you know. Because in them days, rock and roll wasn't happening, the blues wasn't happening, not to the young people had to go to church, you know, and that's all they really was interested in, you know. So I tried music for quite about two or three years and I never could play it. But then I came to New Orleans, and it was years passed, so I got older and older and older, you know. So I went to Los Angeles during the war, World War II, and I was in the hotel business out there, and I made very good money, so I came back and overnight club here in New Orleans. And that's when I got really hooked into the music business.
Well, what did you, what other jobs did you have?
Well, before the music business? Yeah. Well, I was in the Duggars Aircraft during the war time, and after the war, I lived in Buffalo, I worked for Weston House.
During what?
I was a motor inspector for them in Buffalo. Oh. And I was a loomer tester for Duggars Aircraft in New Orleans. I mean, say, in Los Angeles.
Yeah.
So I came back there in our open night club in Coase Quai, and that's-
What was the name of it? The Hurricane. Yeah.

What was that? It was on Claybone Street, South Claybone, 3700 block. Yeah. So we had a very nice club there, and it was small, and we were getting this track, you know, music, you're tracking into the club. Yeah. And I got hooked up in the booking business, you see.
What were the trill?

Well, we had most of all the famous stuff at that time. King Cole was famous then. We had his trill in there. Charles Brown was famous. We had his trill in there. We had another group called Cat in the Field. They was famous in those times. Cat in the Field, yeah. Uh-huh. Lou Mel Morgan, he had a trill. See, we only had trill because the place was small, you see. Right.
How many people would it exist?
A whole about 200, Jim Moise. Right. But it was real fabulous. It was about the status of the city of New Orleans at that time.
What was your competition? What other clubs were?
I didn't have any competition then, but all of them. What year was this? That was 43.
Yeah.

I didn't have any competition, but after that, after we opened up, everybody came along, you know, and caught it behind us. The city got to blooming like a rose, you know? Yeah. So then, but after they closed this camp, they had a camp, the Camp Plotche, which was a port of embarkation. But after they closed the camp, everybody was soldier, the thing was gone, you know, wasn't no money. So I leased the building out to a guy.
You were getting a lot of business from the soldiers?

Well, most of them. Nine percent of my business was soldiers. Nine percent of them was. They bring the girlfriends in, you know, and whatnot. Nine percent of my business was soldiers. So after the camp closed, wasn't our business in the war, you see. Wasn't in the business. So I could see the trend was changing. And I put an ad that had a paper then called the Pitsbutt Corley. Right, right. And I put an ad in the paper that I wanted to lease the building. And the guy from Chicago saw it and came down and leased it. And I went on work for Weston House after that. Of course, he only kept it for about two years. I had to take it back over again. So then I sold the building after that. That's how I got hooked up in the booking business.
Wasn't Frank Pena's club?
No, Frank Pena's club was Doudrop.
Right.
But he was in Viennese way before I was.
Yeah, that's what I'm saying. You said you had one of the only clubs.

Well, but his club didn't compare with ours. Foster had one called the Rainbow Room. Rainbow Room. He didn't compare with us at all. Hydel opened one down here on the highway, which was known as the Roundivou. It was fabulous, but it was too far out. Yeah. Yeah, too far out. The Transitution was like it is now, you see. But his was fabulous. We had the fabulous one. We had the first one brought out these glass bricks with the light behind them. We also had a glass brick bar with the light behind it, you know. And we had all the walls with leatherettes. In the Cedar Bar we had all leatherettes.
Leatherettes?
Yeah, fixed in like cushions on automobiles, you see.
Yeah, on the walls.
On the walls, uh-huh. We had the fabulous place in the city. We really did.
I mean, that's a looking place. Right, right.
And then we was in a good location. Yeah, you were right on the floor. The place on the block, Claybone Street is a good location, you see.
Was, was, uh, you were saying your place was much more popular than Frank's one? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, right definitely.

Frank and the Rainbow Room. Yeah. Both of them, definitely. Yeah. Now Hayes came back. He, he waited too late. He, he had a small little chicken place across the street there on, uh, Dan Hill and, uh,
it was an avenue.
Yeah, it was a chicken. And then he went across the street to build a fabulous place, but he waited too late to build it. See, the camp had closed out. He had a fabulous place too.
Yeah, a lot of people were making money off the, the, the soldiers.

Yeah, that's, that's why your money was, you see. Soldiers coming in town, coming in town, coming in town, this coming town most every night, a lot of them had cars, weren't you know. Right. They were looking for quiet places, nice places to go, you see. Right. And so, Hayes opened his place up for you after, after the camp closed out. Right. And of course I think he lost a lot of money. He had, his place was fabulous too. Yeah. He had carpet, we didn't have carpet on our floor cause carpet wasn't styled on the floor like it is now, you see. Yeah, yeah.
And you always had, had music in the hard time?
I already had music, we always kept trill over and we never charge to come in.
I mean six nights a week?
No, yeah, five, yeah, five nights a week. We changed by five nights. We was open, we never did close. We opened from, uh,
24 hours?
No, no, no, five o'clock till one at night. One at night, we was gone. And no cover charge?
No cover charge, never. But how, how were you driving?

Well, our price was pretty high. Everybody said, come to the organization, say that you have to carry a checkbook to go in there. That's perfect, yes. And of course we had a gimmick with it. We got in with the, conducting on the streetcar, you know, we freeze them off a little. And when they, at that time, they had the Claiborne streetcar instead of the Claiborne bus.
Okay, yeah, the streetcar coming up.

Yeah, the Claiborne's right in the middle of the neutral ground, you see. So when he'd get there, when he would get to Louisiana Avenue in Claiborne, the next stop he would say, General Taylor, you know, next stop General Taylor. And right to your left you see the fabulous hurricane. And he would call, just like a train, call up here, call up on a train, right. And of course we got the business, we had more business than we could take here. We couldn't, we couldn't hold the train. The only thing about it, we'd need a larger place. But during that time, you couldn't buy any lumber. See the lumber's all there, the government had everything on there. Yeah, everything would seal off, you see. So we couldn't make it any bigger. You had to hold what we had. What we used to do, we had a lounge in the front, with some couches that'd sit in there, and people would come in and wait for tables, you know. You and your girlfriend would come in, and we'd just tell you to have a seat at the first table, and then we'd come get you there. That's what you said, but we could have really made more money and better if the place had been bigger. We couldn't buy any lumber.
So when did you really decide to get into this booking? In the booking?

Well after I leased the hurricane, I went to Buffalo and worked for Western House out there for a year and a half I believe it was. And then this fellow foaled up with the club, so I had to come back and take the club over, you see. Take the building over. Then he asked you to come back? Well yeah, he just foaled up, he threw his hand up, he couldn't pay any more rent. So then I came back and I decided, well the best thing I needed to do was to settle and get rid of it, because you know, I wouldn't go into the business anymore. So after I did that, well then I started the booking. I started booking dances and things like that, in different clubs. They had a club then called the Rhythm Club on Jackson Avenue. We used to go there.
Is it still there?
No, it's still there. No, it's just empty lots there. It's a lot there. They'd boink down. And then they'd have the Billy Bates. They'd have the Billy Bates.
Right on Jackson.
Jackson and Dirtwood.
Right on Shakespeare, there's some club that's still in it on the road. Shakespeare Pines? I don't know what that is.
But I know, I know.
You can go look at it.
Yeah. I know this and they told this one.
This is boink down.

So we would go there, from there we'd go to the Gypsy Room down on Arlene Street. Yeah. What's that? They had the, how did they call it the Gypsy Room I believe it was. That's what the name it was. So we'd go there for dances. So then, later on down the line I decided I'd hit the road, do one-nighters. So I started doing one-nighters with just bands, not no artists or nothing, just a local band. You know, here and there and here. And I had a good route. From San Antonio, Texas all the way down into New Orleans and up the all the way to Pensacola, Florida down into Alabama. I had a good route, you know. So I'd be playing for 20 jobs and serology jobs like these college, you know.
Yeah, so you started making your contacts and then once you had your contacts set in a few tabs, you just keep sending bands to them that you were working with.
Yeah. Now I can start to tell you about Slim, because this is time for him to come in right now. So later I met, later I met Gitar Slim.
Wait, who was your first big, your hottest act, your first hot act that you were in? Well, well, somebody trying to get some? Yeah. S-U-P? I'm going. I got it.
Well, actually, let me go in, let me start from Slim on, then I'll bring you in.
Okay, okay, when did you meet Slim? What was it?

I don't remember the year, I don't remember the year now of Hans, I don't remember him, but anyway, Slim came to me. I was living downtown on Utrip Street, and he had three pieces with him. Well, see, I had this band already with about six, seven pieces. So, I told him, I said, well, man, I said, I've got a good band. He said, man, I can improve your business, you know. I said, come over and hear me. I said, I went over, he's working over the river over here then, or the place over there, I can't think of the name of the place. So, he had three pieces with him, a drum, guitar, no, drum, piano, and the saxophone guitar.
Do you know who the band was?

Well, he called it his band, I don't remember the name. You don't remember the band? Yeah, I don't remember the band. I don't remember who was in the band, yes. He had a boy named Harry Smith, which is a minister now.
Yeah.

And then he had another boy named Oscar Moore, used to be like at the Dewdrop for years. I don't remember Oscar, he's a drummer. So what we did, we laid two pieces out, we laid one piece out of the band off, we just laid one piece out of the drummer, so he had a bit of drum in the head. And we just kept the piano player, we made the band a little bigger. So we got to traveling, and we had another little boy with us from here, his name was Eddie Langlois, we called him Billy Eddie, his name was Eddie Langlois. So he was in the band, and him and Slim would work together. They had fifty feet of water on the guitar. Each one had that. So they would walk on top of the bar, walk all on tables, you know. And man, Ben has just got to come in like you're pouring water in a pitcher, you know. Everybody wanted to book that band, you know. You see that little boy on the main walking the tables, walking the bars, and they'd go all outside with the guitar, you wouldn't see them, just hear the music on the stage, you know where he is, he's got a long run, you know. So to make the story start, we just really built up, we got up to, you know, we was in top bracket. So a guy heard us in Monroe, Louisiana, from Nashville, and he went back and told the guy who owned the club in Nashville about this band he heard. We didn't have no records working out, you know. And we played a ballad of blues with Best Domino in Monroe, that's how it was. So this kid called me out of Nashville, and we made a deal. He said, his name was Grady, I don't remember the first name, but he owned Grady's Club on the fourth floor of a building there. He heard something like, Grady. So he called me and told me he would send me transportation, come up to an audition, you know. So I accepted transportation, because what I was going to do, I was going to book myself on the way up there anyway, you see.
Yeah.

So we did, we went on to that term. And the night we got there, Diana Watson and Illinois Jackie was playing. You can remember them, they were playing together. So after they went off, the show went off, and we came on, I don't know, people just went, they went wild and see that guy, that little boy in the main walking the bar with the guitar playing, and then that little boy would get on his shoulders and play together. So the guy told him, he said, man, you got a four weeks contract right now. So I said, well I can't play four weeks, I'll tell you, I can play the first week, I have to go back and play my one nighters out. I said, I'm going to play the first week, we'll take a four weeks contract, but I'm going to play one of them and come back. So he agreed for us. And after that we just stayed in Nashville, you know, off and on, off and on. So I met a guy who had a little record company, I can't think of the name of the record
company, but anyway, he had a record company there.

Yeah, I know who it is, but I can't call it. Yeah, so him and I got together, I said, name, how about Nick? No, the first thing was, Slim wrote a song in his hotel room. He wrote it on one of these laundry bags, remember the laundry bag, you'd be in brown paper. He wrote the whole song, he came in my room and sang the song to me. He said, what are you thinking about it? I said, it's all right. I said, you want to cut it? He said, yeah. I said, well, I'm going to talk to this guy who was at the club last night. He said, well, he said, so I got in touch with the fella, and so he said, well, look, man, I ain't got no money. He said, I'll press the record and release it if you pay the band off. I said, okay. So I bought the deal. He didn't have a studio. He had a big tape recorder, on there tape recorder. And he went somewhere and got some old bags, you know these bags where they put around, tighten them on the deal and tighten up, it's clean like a bag. And he had stuff all on the floor, all hung up beside the wall, just in that little room. With a small tape recorder, you know. And we cut the first session on Slim there. Feeling Sad. I tell the story. I remember the name. Ray Charles Cuttergold after he did. So that was the first starting of him.
Well, that record just really went tough off.

It really took off. People knew who he was, you know, and he was behind it. So this guy didn't have any money, and his publishing wasn't right. Everything behind him was all together wrong. It wasn't out he was trying to steal, but he just didn't have the set out. So I told Slim, I said, now the best thing for us to do is not to go back to the couple of the sets. We had no contract with him, nothing. I said, of course, he's not going to be able to give us the right distributor on the record, and we're not going to be able to get the right pay off on the record. So we might as well just figure we got this to start off. So then they had a company out of California special director. So I got in touch with a boy out of Jackson, Mississippi work for special. His name was Johnny Denson. In fact, Johnny Denson later started out of the business. He was a business manager. He was a business manager. He wasn't out he was trying to steal but he just didn't have the set out. So I told Slim, I said, now the best thing for us to do is not to go back to the company. We had no contract with him, nothing. I said, of course, he's not going to be able to give us the right distributor on the record. And we're not going to be able to get the right pay off on the record. In fact, John, if that's the latest artist in the company after that, the Zoom set after that, he recorded Hugh Smith in the column after that, I'm doing labor. So they sent, the guys sent him up here and we heard him and then we recorded him. And that was the thing that I used to do. And it really bloomed, it really went over.
Now, didn't you, when did you stop booking Smith?

What happened after we cut the second record, or the thing that I used to do, well then it was time for a new contract. So maybe by then I'll tell you this on the tape, maybe I can't tell you. So after then, Frank Penae wrapped him up. He tucked him because I didn't have, my contract was out and he wouldn't renew it.
He wouldn't renew the contract. Now wait, now I didn't, I didn't bring the article with me, but I found something. Were you sued Slim? Right, right, right, right.

He wouldn't honor Hugh Smith? Right, well see what happened, he left before, he had about say two months on his contract. And see, my lawyer said that we still could hold him because the contract had expired. He had already given me a notice he wasn't going to sign me. He just told me he had somebody to sign, see. But he still had to honor my contract up to the last minute. And that's what he didn't do, so that's why we entered a suit against him.
So you had booked him a number of dates and then he didn't honor him? He didn't honor him. He didn't pay the date. You lost that after that. Remember the figure was $4,600.
We got $4,000 out of it. Shaw always paid off. Shaw paid off $4,000.
Because he signed with Shaw after he signed with Shaw before my contract was even up.

And that's what we really had, that's what he was really scared of, you see. Right. Well that wasn't a lot of pay. Shaw had a lot of good odds in those days. They were making a lot of money, you know. They flew the guy in here and brought me a check. We didn't have to go to the coach. We just, well we filed a suit against him. And when they filed a suit against him, they paid off in a sweats, you know. So that was the biggest artist that I recorded. I mean, that's what I won't get down to. That was the biggest one that I recorded was get slim. And of course the next big artist I recorded was a girl named Alma Thomas, which is here now. I recorded her. She had her number, which one would care. She stayed with me for about four or five years. And of course she met her new husband and the husband took over the business. I never had a contract with her. I never had a contract with her.
So, let's go back to Slim. When, when, how, do you know anything about how, we'll get to a few things, how Slim, how Slim died?

No, I don't. No more than what Ewe Smith told me that, I think he said he died in his sleep. I really don't know about his death too much. I really don't know. But he was in Ohio. I don't know. Slim was a heavy drinker. Very heavy drinker. And of course I'm quite sure after he started making heavy money, I guess he started drinking heavy, you know. But I think they find him in the sleeper. I'm almost sure. I wouldn't, I wouldn't, I wouldn't bet on him, but I think this way it was. Because he was in Ohio, and I talked to him here, because they brought him back there, I think, and buried him in the Thibodeau. Now, now Frank Pena didn't have him then. Another guy by the name of Hosey Hill had him. Hosey had got him from Frank. Somebody Hosey twisted him with Frank some kind of way. But Hosey and Frank was very good friends. I don't know what went down the line. But Hosey had him at that particular time. Frank didn't have him when he died. Because Hosey brought him back to bed. But I don't think he had any money when he died. I think he was broke. Yeah. I think he wasn't going down. Thank you.
Do you know anything about his family?
I met his family in Hollandale, Mississippi. That's where his hometown. We used to play that all the time.
Where would you play in Hollandale? At this hometown?
Yeah. Why we played there? We played there because he wanted to go home after he had got famous.
He would want to go there periodically? Yeah, to play. To play.

And of course he drew a packed house. He drew all the time around, because all of them knew him around there. So we played there several times. And if I'm not mistaken, I think we played there on our way to Memphis. I'm almost sure we're there. If we're in Nashville, I'm almost sure we're there. That was pretty long ago. Uh-huh. So I think we played that time. And we played there. I met his mother was dead. His grandmother raised her. Uh-huh. Do you remember her name? Huh? I don't remember her name. I really don't. But I met her and she told me what's happening and said, you know, he'd never send her no money. And from that day on until I got rid of him, I used to mail her money out every Saturday, each year a month. I mail her check each month. So how her name? Yeah. But I can't tell you her name. I don't remember.
It's been quite some time, you know. Was it Jones or what? Do you think it was? I don't remember. Did he have any brothers or sisters?

I think he had a brother. I think he had one brother. He had a lot of nephews, nieces and what. I can't recall whether he had a sister. I could have met her sister there. I really don't remember. It's been quite some time, you know. Yeah, he might have had a sister. I know he had a brother. I met her brother. A lot of nieces and nephews. I met them. I met cousins and what not. But I remember this lady. I went to her house. The first time we played there, I went to her house and I met her. She sat down and told me, you know, his mother died when he was young and she had raised him. He know you don't send her nothing. She was getting the age on her, you know. So I told her, I said, well look, as long as I manage him, as long as I'm booking him, you'll get some money from me. I used to mail up checking money. He didn't reject. He didn't reject. He didn't. He didn't, I mean he didn't. He didn't reject me $10,000 money. He didn't reject it, you know. Oh, okay. He wouldn't send it himself? No, he didn't send it. I guess he figured, well, since you're going to have the job, you go do it yourself, you know. But if I took out $50 out of his check, that money, he wouldn't say nothing about it. I just tell him. I took $50 out of his check, you know. What type of person was Slim? Slim was a good fellow. Like I said, he was a heavy drinker. And I never had any trouble with him. You know, like if I tell him we have to leave town at the same time, or if I tell him to do a certain show, or don't want to make the show too long, he listened. You know, I didn't have any trouble out of him. He was crazy, he listened up. I think really what happened, the lot, why he did have left me. I think Frank came in. You see, Shaw wanted him. And they didn't, they contacted Frank, because Frank was doing business with him, buying artists from him. So I think Frank come in and showed him the place that he's going to buy him a 747 jet, you know, and that type of blip, blip, blip. I think that's why he left. I think that's why he left. And I don't make promise nothing I can't do, so I didn't promise nothing.
You were one man, through a one man agency. It was Shaw, with a lot of money in the money.

A lot of money. See, so what they went and got some money from Shaw and got out of my Oldsmobile, you see. So I guess that was the deal, you know. But I never had the trouble out of him, you know. I never had the trouble out of him. When I said ready to go, and I said it was going, it was time to go on, you know. If I said we're not going to stop at such a time, we're going to stop next time, he never grumbled out at all. He always looked at me like if he thought I knew what was happening, you know. I really was sorry when I found that it was, I knew it was going to happen to him, because, you see what I did when I was the manager, I only gave him the same amount of money and put the rest of it in the bank for him. And I had it so he couldn't draw it unless I gave him some of it, you see. So I guess when the other guy's taking him over, you know, they just give his money the game, obviously. So I guess it's interesting.

Sometimes they'll take it off the top and they don't know how much they're actually paying. Right, right, right. That's what happened. How do you treat people in his band? Somebody told me he had sort of an ego problem. Did you find that?

I don't think so. I don't think he did. I mean, you know, he got along with the members of the band, alright, because they're always drinking. He was drinking and the member of the band was drinking, you know. So I don't think he, you might have, you see, he was a musician, he didn't know music. He only played by, yeah, you know, and he used a thing on his guitar called a choker. And if they took that choker he couldn't go on. Well sometimes they'd do it just to kick something, hide it, you know, almost time for him to go on. And then he'd come to me and say, hey, got my choker, so he got to get it, he got to get it. Well then I'd tell him, I'd threat the band, you're using a given choker, I ain't gonna pay you off, you know. So that's what happened, but he got along with them alright, I don't think he had no trouble with them. Him and Hewlett Smith was tight because they used to be room buddies, you know. Hewlett used to call him Poor Devil. Come on, answer the door for me.
Used to call him Poor Devil?

Yeah, Poor Devil. And he used to call Hewlett Death. Hewlett was so puny looking, you know, and he never would get up, when he'd go to bed at night from the, yeah, he never'd get the time to get up. He'd never get the time to go to the gig next year, he wouldn't get the heat or nothing, just to rent a bed all day. So Slim used to call him Death, and Hewlett called him Poor Devil.
He used to call his guitar that, he used to call his guitar the Devil. Yeah, yeah. What do you know about Ray Charles?

Well, Ray was a good friend of mine, was a good friend of mine. I knew when he started out, I remember when he used to travel, he came in his band and arrived in a little, at that time they used to make a little car called a disorder stage with a rag on the top, because all the band was buying him, you know. He had a little stuff placed in their back. And Ray used to come to Pensacola, I used to come to Pensacola, we used to play around Alabama and Pensacola pretty often. So Ray would come in there, and I met him one day, and we got to be friends. But, and I booked Ray, I used to pay Ray $350 a night, $400 a night. I used to book him off and off. We used to book him off and off. We used to work in New York together. We used to travel with a boy named D. Clark then. And we was in the same hotel together. So I booked him. And last time I booked him, he was $5,000. I lost money on him. I have never made money. I didn't make money when I paid him for $350 a night. I couldn't make money on him. I played him all around New York and couldn't draw a card away. I came to Pensacola at the Auditore. When he was $5,000, I lost money on him. So I told him that night, I said, I don't know you or no me, so we left it off. But I never could make money with him.
New Orleans, you mean he just worked in?
